::: {.why}
Choosing a container by its complexity class alone is how you end up with an asymptotically optimal book that is slower than an array, and knowing why is a standard interview subject.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Choose the right container for an order book's two access patterns and defend each choice.
- Say when a vector beats a hash map despite worse complexity, and demonstrate it.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Measure the constant factors: time lookups in a vector, a sorted vector with binary search, an unordered map and an ordered map, across sizes from 8 to 100,000 elements. Plot time against size for all four. Below a few hundred elements the linear scan over a contiguous vector usually wins, and that crossover point is the thing to know.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Apply it to the design: an order book has few price levels near the touch and many orders, so the price levels want a sorted contiguous structure and the order lookup wants a hash map. Write the design down with the reasoning attached, since it is exactly the question that gets asked.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
Lookup timings for four containers across six sizes with the crossover identified, plus a written order book data structure design.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Why might a linear scan over a vector beat a hash map lookup, and at roughly what size does that stop being true?
:::
